summary: This memo revisits network capacity metrics first examined in RFC 5136. It defines a more practical Maximum IP-Layer Capacity Metric that is suited to measurement, and outlines the corresponding methods of measurement.

plainLanguage.summary: How much can a pipe carry at most? This document defines how to measure the biggest amount of data that can flow one way across a network.

questions: how to measure one-way ip capacity
what is maximum ip layer capacity
how to measure one way ip capacity
how does the load rate adjustment algorithm work
what are the default measurement parameters for ip capacity
subtitle: Defines Maximum IP-Layer Capacity, a practical way to measure the most data a network path can carry one way, plus a UDP-based method for measuring it.

tldr.problem: Subscribers, providers and others want to check that an access network really delivers the speed it was sold at, and earlier capacity definitions were hard to apply as practical measurements.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines IP-Layer Capacity as bits per second counted over short equal sub-intervals, with Maximum IP-Layer Capacity as the largest such value that still meets chosen loss or delay targets. A Sender ramps its UDP load up and down based on feedback from the Receiver to find that maximum.
tldr.outcome: It gives the industry one metric and one method for short diagnostic tests, with required parameters, reporting formats and safety limits. The load adjustment algorithm must not be used as a general congestion control algorithm.

today: RFC 9097 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It builds on the earlier capacity work in RFC 5136 and the IPPM framework of RFC 2330.

sections.title: Why Measure Maximum Capacity
sections.content:
The IETF has worked on network capacity metrics for over twenty years, including RFC 3148 (Bulk Transport Capacity), RFC 5136 (Network Capacity and Maximum IP-Layer Capacity) and the experimental RFC 8337. This memo revisits the problem and defines a more practical Maximum IP-Layer Capacity metric. The RFC says it is like the theoretical goal for goodput, and is a different metric from Bulk Transfer Capacity.

The main use case is checking a network where the subscriber gets specific performance assurances. If a user subscribes to a 1 Gbps service, the user and the provider want to confirm that rate is delivered, and if it is, a tester can look for a bottleneck elsewhere.

The RFC lists five changes in the 2013-2019 time frame that affect measurement design: access is no longer the bottleneck for many users, both transfer rate and latency matter, UDP's role is growing, content is moving closer to users, and there is less emphasis on ISP gateway measurements.
sections.plainLanguage: If you pay for a fast connection, you want a fair way to check you really get it. This document defines that check.

sections.title: Scope and Limits
sections.content:
The metrics use active measurement: test packets are sent on purpose, rather than watching user traffic. The focus is the access portion of the network, as in RFC 7497.

The load rate adjustment algorithm is for infrequent, diagnostic, short-term measurement only. It MUST NOT be used as a general congestion control algorithm, and it MUST only be used for diagnostic and operations measurements. It is RECOMMENDED to stop other non-measurement traffic on the subscriber's dedicated resources while testing.

The measurement system's algorithm SHALL NOT be told the exact capacity value in advance. The RFC says this keeps results fair and removes an opportunity for nefarious operation enabled by knowing the answer.
sections.plainLanguage: This test is a short check-up, not something to run all the time. And the tester is not allowed to peek at the answer first.

sections.title: Parameters and Defaults
sections.content:
Every metric starts from a shared list of input parameters. The key ones are the source and destination (Src, Dst), MaxHops (a limit implemented in the TTL or Hop Limit), the measurement interval I and its equal sub-intervals dt, the feedback interval FT, and the number of flows F.

Defaults are I = 10 seconds, dt = 1 second, FT = 50 msec and one flow. Tmax is a maximum waiting time long enough to tell delayed packets from lost ones. PM is a list of metrics such as loss and delay with target thresholds, and at least one must be supplied (for example one-way packet loss equal to zero).

A flow is the stream of packets with the same designated header fields, so that they get identical treatment in multipath decisions such as load balancing. Test packets must use UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: Before testing you decide how long to test, how often to check in, and what counts as 'good enough', like too many lost packets.

sections.title: The Metrics
sections.content:
IP-Layer Capacity (formally Type-P-One-way-IP-Capacity) is the number of IP-layer bits, counting header and data, that can be sent from the Src host and correctly received by the Dst host during one sub-interval dt, divided by dt. All sub-intervals MUST be equal in length.

Maximum IP-Layer Capacity (Type-P-One-way-Max-IP-Capacity) is the maximum of that value over all dt-length sub-intervals in the interval, among those meeting the PM criteria. If several targets are set, the best sub-interval must meet all of them. The physical interface of the measurement devices MUST be faster than the smallest link on the path, the bottleneck.

A third metric, IP-Layer Sender Bit Rate, is measured at the Source and checks that the Sender actually produced the intended rates. It is not a path performance metric. Related round-trip delay and one-way loss are collected alongside, and other metrics such as reordering and delay variation MAY be measured.

A maximum with no sign of congestion (rising latency, loss or ECN marks) is likely an underestimate. Shapers and policers can also inflate results, so different dt values SHOULD be tried when traffic conditioning is expected.
sections.plainLanguage: Cut the test into small slices of time, count how much got through in each slice, and take the best slice that still looked healthy.

sections.title: The Load Rate Adjustment Algorithm
sections.content:
The test administrator pre-builds a table of offered load rates. It is RECOMMENDED to start with 0.5 Mbps at index zero, 1 Mbps at index one, then 1 Mbps steps up to 1 Gbps, 100 Mbps steps up to 10 Gbps and 1 Gbps steps above that. The Sender starts at rate R1. The Receiver checks arriving datagrams for sequence number anomalies and measures the delay range, then sends a status feedback message every FT.

  • No anomalies and delay below the lower threshold: increase the rate. Before congestion is confirmed the jump is more than one step (for example Rx+10); afterwards it is one step.
  • Anomalies, or delay above the upper threshold: decrease the rate. The first time congestion is confirmed the drop is larger (for example Rx-30); otherwise it is one step.
  • No anomalies and delay between the two thresholds: leave the rate unchanged.

Recommended thresholds are 10 for sequence number gaps and 30 msec and 90 msec for the lower and upper delay thresholds. Congestion is inferred when anomalies or high delay appear for three consecutive feedback intervals. If feedback messages stop arriving, the Sender also reduces its load, and timers stop the test if packets or feedback cease unexpectedly.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender speeds up while everything looks fine, slows down when messages start getting lost or late, and holds steady when it is unsure.

sections.title: Qualifying and Running Tests
sections.content:
Equipment must be calibrated so it can measure the expected capacity. Artificially high values can appear until a buffer on the path fills, so the RFC describes a qualification run: a later measurement sending at a fixed 99.x percent of the Maximum IP-Layer Capacity, which passes if there are no supra-threshold losses and no growing minimum delay trend.

Test duration must be kept short because the test likely causes congestion. Ten-second tests per direction are described as common. The RFC contrasts this with the throughput method of RFC 2544, which can cause sustained overload, a concern raised in RFC 6815.

Other rules include setting MaxHops from the expected path length, sequence numbers in both load packets and feedback messages, a short preamble to wake on-demand access links, and no more than one concurrent independent test on a path. Multiple flows may help when link aggregation or per-type policies are present, each with its own algorithm instance.
sections.plainLanguage: After finding the best speed, the tester runs again just under it to make sure it really holds up, and keeps every test short so nobody's internet suffers.

sections.title: Reporting and Security
sections.content:
Capacity should be reported in Mbps, defined as 1,000,000 bits per second, with at least single-Megabit resolution, together with the related loss and round-trip delay. If the path shows repeatable modes (for example a 'turbo mode' that speeds short transfers), each mode SHALL be reported. Results are shown in a table with test phase, number of flows, capacity, loss ratio and RTT minimum and maximum. The Broadband Forum's TR-471 provides an information model for configuration and reporting.

For safety, the RFC REQUIRES cooperating Source and Destination hosts with agreement to test, and a client-initiated setup handshake so firewalls can control unsolicited UDP. Authentication and integrity protection of feedback messages are RECOMMENDED. Hosts MUST limit simultaneous tests, Senders MUST be rate limited, and testing against a provider's hosts SHOULD be limited in frequency or volume. The RFC leaves exact protocol specifications to future work and has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must agree to the test, the sender is never allowed to blast at full speed from the start, and the results are written up in a clear table.

messages.label: Load datagrams at rate Rx
messages.note: The test starts at rate R1 from the pre-built table.

messages.label: Status feedback every FT
messages.note: Reports sequence anomalies and the delay range; the default FT is 50 msec.

messages.label: Load at adjusted rate
messages.note: Raised, lowered or kept according to the feedback.

viz.caption: HOW FEEDBACK CHANGES THE OFFERED LOAD

cells: No anomalies, delay below lower threshold (30 msec)
Increase: more than one step before congestion is confirmed, else one step
Anomalies, or delay above upper threshold (90 msec)
Decrease: larger drop when congestion is first confirmed, else one step
No anomalies, delay between the thresholds
